title: PARGAN SINGH versus STATE OF PUNJAB & ANR.
case_title: Pargan Singh v. State of Punjab
confession: Extra-judicial confession by appellants to PW-1, corroborated by eye-witnesses
aggravating_circumstances: Death of victim, serious injury to PW-2, traumatic experience for PW-2
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under sections 302, 307, 397 IPC read with Section 34 IPC
neutral_facts: The prosecution case was that on 25.03.1999, two individuals on a scooter fired at the victim-deceased and snatched a money bag from him. When PW-2 tried to stop them, he was also shot. The assailants fled away. The victim-deceased was found dead at the scene, and PW-2 was injured. The police could not identify the culprits for several years until information led to the arrest of the two accused-appellants. The accused were identified by eyewitnesses PW-2 and PW-3, who described the incident in detail. PW-2, the injured witness, testified that the accused shot the victim-deceased and then fired at him before fleeing. The incident lasted for 90 seconds, and PW-2 became unconscious after being shot. The medical evidence confirmed the injuries were caused by a firearm. The accused refused to participate in the identification parade, but the courts accepted the eyewitness accounts and the medical evidence as credible.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment and fine of Rs.50,000/- each and in default of payment of fine, they have to undergo further rigorous imprisonment for two years. For conviction under Section 307 IPC read with Section 34 IPC, sentence of 10 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.25,000/- is imposed and in default of payment of fine, they have to undergo further rigorous imprisonment for one year. Likewise, for offences under Section 397 IPC, rigorous imprisonment for a period of 10 years is imposed.
physical_harm: The victim-deceased was shot dead and PW-2 sustained multiple lacerated wounds, including injuries to the right shoulder, neck, lower leg, chin, right eye, and tongue, resulting in severe haemorrhage and shock.
number_of_offences: Three offences/counts charged and finally upheld: Sections 302, 307, and 397 IPC read with Section 34 IPC.
financial_property_loss: Rs. 4 lakhs was snatched from the victim-deceased.
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the testimony of PW-2 and PW-3 as credible eye-witnesses, and the extra-judicial confession of the appellants made before PW-1, who was the Pradhan of his Mohalla.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that PW-2, an injured eye-witness, had a traumatic experience which made it unlikely he would forget the faces of the accused, and that the version of PW-2 and PW-3 was consistent and corroborated by medical evidence.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 25.03.1999; Trial judgment: 25.09.2008; High Court decision: 13.12.2012; Supreme Court decision: 05.09.2014
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: A.Tiwari, Eliza Bar, Shree Pal Singh, Shiv kumar Suri, Shikhil Suri; Counsel for the State: V. Madhukar, AAG, Anvita Cowshish, Kuldip Singh
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction upheld; High Court: Conviction upheld; Supreme Court: Appeals dismissed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellants were the perpetrators of the crime, as evidenced by the eyewitness accounts of PW-2 and PW-3, and that the appellants had confessed to the crime before PW-1, who was a respected community leader.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the appellants could not be identified after 7 years due to the passage of time and the lack of previous acquaintance with the witnesses, and that the testimony of PW-2 was unreliable due to the lapse of time and the possibility of memory fading.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that memory is not a video recorder and that the circumstances under which an event is witnessed significantly affect the reliability of the memory, especially in cases involving trauma and severe injury.
precedent_relied_upon: Balwinder Singh v. State of Punjab (1995) Supp (4) SCC 259
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed due to the conviction under sections 302, 307, and 397 IPC, read with Section 34 IPC, based on the credible eyewitness accounts and the serious nature of the crime, including the death of the victim and the injury to PW-2.

title: DR. VINOD BHANDARI versus STATE OF M.P.
case_title: Dr. Vinod Bhandari v. State of M.P.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.420, s.467, s.468, s.471, s.120B; Madhya Pradesh Manyata Prapt Pariksha Adhiniyam, 1937 s.3(d), s.1, s.2/4; IT Act s.65, s.66
trial_court_outcome: Bail application dismissed
neutral_facts: The accused, a managing director of a medical institute, was involved in a large-scale scam where he colluded with officials of a professional examination board to admit undeserving candidates to medical courses through corrupt means. The accused received money from candidates through intermediaries for arranging unfair admission. Evidence included recovered documents, financial records, and statements from witnesses indicating the accused's role in the conspiracy. The investigation involved a significant number of accused and witnesses, with substantial evidence collected against the accused. The trial was delayed, and the accused had been in custody for over a year. The courts considered the seriousness of the allegations, the potential impact on the medical profession, and the risk of trial being influenced by granting bail. The accused's actions were alleged to have caused significant financial loss to the state and undermined public trust in the medical profession.
physical_harm: Not stated
number_of_offences: 516 accused, 329 arrested, 187 pending arrest
premeditation_planning: Yes, the court found premeditation/planning in the form of a well-designed conspiracy
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the evidence that the appellant, Dr. Vinod Bhandari, was involved in a conspiracy to illegally admit undeserving candidates to medical courses through corrupt means, including receiving money from candidates, colluding with Vyapam officials, and facilitating unfair exam practices.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that the allegations were supported by material on record, including documents, seized funds, and statements from co-accused individuals.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant had gone abroad soon after the registration of the crime and returned to India only after being granted anticipatory bail, indicating a potential attempt to avoid arrest.

title: N PARAMESWARAN UNNI versus G KANNAN AND ANOTHER
case_title: N Parameswaran Unni v. G Kannan and Another
statutory_provisions: Negotiable Instruments Act s.138 rlw. s.142
trial_court_outcome: Convicted and sentenced to simple imprisonment of three months
offence_finally_established: Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act
neutral_facts: The accused borrowed a total of Rs. 64,000 from the complainant and issued three cheques, two of which were returned by the bank as dishonoured. The complainant received an intimation from the bank about the dishonour of the cheques on 08.04.1991. The complainant issued a legal notice to the accused on 12.04.1991, which was returned with a postal endorsement indicating the addressee was absent. The complainant sent another legal notice on 04.05.1991, which was returned with a postal endorsement indicating it was refused. The complainant then filed a complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.
offence_severity: imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both
physical_harm: Not stated
number_of_offences: Two cheques dishonoured, complaint filed under Section 138, upheld by Trial Court and Appellate Court
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the first notice sent by the appellant on 12-04-1991 was deemed to have been served on the first respondent, and that the second notice was a reminder of the respondent's obligation to discharge his liability.
witness_credibility: Not stated
trial_duration: {'dates_of_offence': '13-10-1990', 'trial_judgment': '29-07-1993', 'high_court_decision': '07-07-1995', 'supreme_court_decision': '06-10-2003'}
legal_representation: {'accused': 'M. Gireesh Kumar, Sriram P., Ms. Athira G. Nair (for Ankur S. Kulkarni)', 'state': 'C. K. Sasi, Manu Krishnan G., Abraham Mathews (for P. V. Dinesh)'}
investigation_status: Complaint filed under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, trial completed
appeal_history: {'trial_court': 'Convicted and sentenced the first respondent to undergo simple imprisonment of three months', 'high_court': 'Allowed the criminal revision of the first respondent by setting aside the concurrent judgments of Trial Court and Appellate Court', 'supreme_court': 'Set aside the impugned judgment of the High Court'}
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the first respondent failed to return the borrowed amount Rs. 64,000/- for which statutory notice under proviso (b) of Section 138 of the N.I. Act was issued to him to make good the dishonoured cheques due to insufficiency of funds in his bank account. The appellant lodged a private complaint before the Judicial First Class Magistrate-II, Alappuzha for the alleged offence under Section 138 of the N.I. Act.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the provisions of Section 138 of the N.I. Act cannot be invoked as the appellant had not complied with the conditions in Clause (b) of the proviso to the said section. Notice demanding payment of the amount arising from the two dishonoured cheques in question was on 04-05-1991, whereas the intimation regarding dishonour of the said cheques was given by the appellant's bank on 08-04-1991. Therefore, the notice was beyond 15 days.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that once notice is sent by registered post by correctly addressing to the drawer of the cheque, the service of notice is deemed to have been effected. The Court also emphasized that the object of providing Clause (c) of Section 138 is to avoid unnecessary hardship and that the right of an honest lender cannot be defeated.
precedent_relied_upon: Mis. New India Sugar Mills Ltd. v. Commissioner of Sales Tax AIR 1963 SC 1207; Jagdish Singh v. Natthu Singh (1992) 1 SCC 647; State of MP v. Hiralal (1996) 7 SCC 523; V. Raja Kumari v. P. Subbarama Naidu (2004) 8 SCC 774
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the complaint was filed within the stipulated time contemplated under Clause (b) of Section 142 of the N.I. Act, therefore, Section 138 read with 142 of N.I. Act is attracted.
other_sentence_order: The Court directed the first respondent to deposit Rs. 2,00,000/- before the Judicial First Class Magistrate-II at Alappuzha on or before 30.04.2017. Out of the said amount, Rs.1,30,000/- shall be paid to the appellant as compensation. In the event the first respondent fails to deposit the said amount within the stipulated period, the conviction and sentence of three months awarded by the Trial Court shall stand restored and bail granted to the first respondent shall stand cancelled.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused borrowed a total of Rs. 64,000 from the complainant and issued three cheques, two of which were returned by the bank as dishonoured. The complainant received an intimation from the bank about the dishonour of the cheques on 08.04.1991. The complainant issued a legal notice to the accused on 12.04.1991, which was returned with a postal endorsement indicating the addressee was absent. The complainant sent another legal notice on 04.05.1991, which was returned with a postal endorsement indicating it was refused. The complainant then filed a complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. The Trial Court convicted the accused, and the Appellate Court upheld the conviction. The High Court reversed the conviction, arguing that the second notice was sent beyond the 15-day limit. The Supreme Court overturned the High Court's decision, finding that the first notice was valid and the second notice was merely a reminder.

title: MAHADEVAPPA versus STATE OF KARNATAKA REP. BY PUBLIC PROSECUTOR
respondent: STATE OF KARNATAKA REP. BY PUBLIC PROSECUTOR
case_title: MAHADEVAPPA v. STATE OF KARNATAKA REP. BY PUBLIC PROSECUTOR
aggravating_circumstances: Demand of dowry, ill-treatment, assault, addiction to liquor, presence of kerosene oil bottle, burn injuries on upper body
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted
neutral_facts: The accused, a newlywed husband, was addicted to alcohol and frequently demanded money from his wife and her parents. He also subjected his wife to physical abuse and harassment. The wife eventually suffered severe burn injuries and died as a result. The prosecution presented evidence indicating that the accused poured kerosene oil on his wife and set her on fire. The incident occurred in the house where only the accused and the deceased were present. The deceased's body showed signs of burn injuries on the upper part, and kerosene oil was found on her body. A kerosene oil bottle was also found in the room. The deceased's family and relatives testified about the accused's behavior and the circumstances leading to her death. The prosecution argued that the accused's actions were intentional and not accidental.
offence_severity: Minimum 7 years, Maximum 10 years for Section 498A; Minimum 10 years, Maximum 10 years for Section 302
physical_harm: Burn injuries resulting in death
number_of_offences: Two offences charged (Section 498A and 302), both upheld
premeditation_planning: The court found premeditation/planning as the appellant's behavior and actions were part of a pattern of harassment and financial demands
key_evidence_accepted: The evidence of four prosecution witnesses clearly proved that the appellant was addicted to consuming liquor, used to demand money from the deceased and her parents, and at times ill-treated and assaulted the deceased. The presence of kerosene oil on the deceased's body and in the room, along with the nature of burn injuries, supported the conclusion that the appellant was responsible for her death.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses (the father and mother of the deceased) as credible, stating that they are the most natural and material witnesses to speak on such issues. Their evidence was corroborated by their relatives, and there was no contradiction in their testimony despite lengthy cross-examination.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 02.10.1995; Trial judgment: 31.05.2000; High Court decision: 03.01.2007; Supreme Court decision: 07.01.2019
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Mallikarjun S. Mylar, Manjunath, Ms.Umme Salma, Ms. E. R. Sumathy Advs.; Counsel for the State: Joseph Aristotle S., Mrs.Priya Aristotle, Shiva P., Ms. Aruna Hannah Dutta, Ms. Anitha Shenoy, Advs.
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Acquittal; High Court: Conviction; Supreme Court: Dismissed appeal
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant poured kerosene on his wife and set her on fire, resulting in her death. The evidence of four prosecution witnesses clearly proved that the appellant was addicted to liquor, frequently demanded money from the deceased and her parents, and ill-treated and assaulted the deceased. The deceased's death was homicidal, not accidental, and the appellant was the only person present at the time of the incident.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the deceased's sari accidentally caught fire while she was boiling water on the oven, resulting in her death. They claimed it was an accidental death and that the prosecution's case was not sufficiently proven.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that the conduct of the accused towards his wife, including repeated harassment, demand for dowry, and ill-treatment, fell within the meaning of Section 498-A IPC. The court also determined that the death was homicidal, not accidental, based on the evidence.
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the evidence clearly proved the appellant's guilt under Sections 498-A and 302 IPC beyond reasonable doubt. The court found that the deceased's death was homicidal and that the appellant was solely responsible for her death.

The incident occurred in the house where only the accused and the deceased were present. The deceased's body showed signs of burn injuries on the upper part, and kerosene oil was found on her body. A kerosene oil bottle was also found in the room. The deceased's family and relatives testified about the accused's behavior and the circumstances leading to her death. The prosecution argued that the accused's actions were intentional and not accidental.

title: STATE OF A. P. versus M. SOHAN BABU & ANR.
case_title: State of A. P. v. M. Sohan Babu & Anr.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.34; IPC s.460; IPC s.324
aggravating_circumstances: Accused entered the house at midnight with intent to commit robbery; accused were armed with knives and used them repeatedly and effectively; accused caused injuries to the victim and other witnesses; accused threatened neighbours with dire consequences
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under Sections 302/34, 460 and 324 of the Indian Penal Code
high_court_outcome: Converted conviction under Section 302 to one under Section 304 (Part-I) IPC
neutral_facts: The accused entered the house of the victim at midnight. A scuffle ensued between the accused and the victim, during which the accused stabbed the victim in the abdomen and thighs. The victim, who was a physically strong individual, managed to pin the accused to the ground. The accused then used a knife to stab the victim, causing fatal injuries. The accused also inflicted injuries on other witnesses present at the scene and threatened them with dire consequences. The accused were apprehended by the neighbours and handed over to the police. The victim succumbed to his injuries after being taken to the hospital.
physical_harm: Death of the victim, injuries to the deceased and to the witnesses
number_of_offences: Three offences charged (302, 460, 324), all upheld
premeditation_planning: The court found premeditation/planning as the accused entered the house armed with the intention of committing robbery
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the accused, who were armed, entered the house of the victims at midnight with the intention of committing robbery and that A-2 stabbed the deceased on the abdomen and thighs, causing his death.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the witnesses, including P.W. 1 to 4, and relied on their testimony to establish the sequence of events and the injuries caused to the deceased and others.
post_offence_conduct: The accused were overpowered by the neighbours, tied up with a rope, and information was sent to the police. The accused were brought to the ground floor and later apprehended.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 20th/21st November, 1991; Trial judgment: 11.12.2003; High Court decision: Not stated; Supreme Court decision: December 14, 2010
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: I. Venkatanarayana, Ramesh Allanki, D. Mahesh Babu; Counsel for the State: Anil Kumar Tandale, Manoj C. Mishra, Brajesh Jha
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted under Sections 302/34, 460 and 324 of the Indian Penal Code; High Court: Converted conviction under Section 302 to Section 304 Part I; Supreme Court: Set aside High Court's judgment and restored trial court's judgment
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the two accused, who were armed, entered the house of the victims at midnight with the intention of committing robbery. They caused fatal injuries to the deceased and also injured other witnesses, which indicates a clear intention to cause death.
defence_argument: The defence argued that there was no common intention on the part of the accused to commit murder. They claimed that the deceased's death was an unfortunate accident resulting from the accused's attempt to extricate themselves from the deceased's grip during a scuffle.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that the common intention to commit murder can be inferred from the circumstances of the case, even if it arises during an incident, and that the initial purpose of robbery does not preclude the intention to cause death if the accused used weapons effectively.
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the High Court's observation that the matter fell under Section 304 Part I and not Section 302 of the IPC was found to be erroneous. The trial court's conviction under Sections 302/34, 460 and 324 was restored.

title: CHOTKAU versus STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH

When the girl did not return home, a search was conducted, and her dead body was found in a sugarcane field. A villager claimed to have seen the accused leaving the field shortly after. physical_harm: Death caused
number_of_offences: Charged with 2 offences, 2 upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the circumstantial evidence and the last seen theory, but found the testimonies of the prosecution witnesses to be untrustworthy due to serious contradictions.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses (PWs 1 to 3) as completely untrustworthy due to serious contradictions in their evidence, which the Sessions Court and High Court trivialized.

title: KILAKKATHA PARAMBATH SASI & ORS. versus STATE OF KERALA
case_title: KILAKKATHA PARAMBATH SASI & ORS. v. STATE OF KERALA
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted
neutral_facts: The accused, who were part of an unlawful assembly, assaulted the victim and his brother at a bus stand due to political animosity. The victim sustained grievous injuries and later died in the hospital. The prosecution presented evidence from multiple witnesses, including the victim's brother, who described the incident and the weapons used. The victim's brother was examined by a doctor who found multiple incised wounds on him. The deceased's body was subjected to a post-mortem, which revealed 58 injuries, most of which were incised and cutting wounds. The accused were charged with offenses under Sections 147, 148, 307, 324, and 302 of the IPC.
physical_harm: PW-1 was grievously injured with three incised wounds, and his brother died from 58 injuries, most of them incised and cutting wounds
number_of_offences: Charged under Sections 147, 148, 307, 324 and 302 read with Section 149; four accused were finally upheld
motive: Political animosity between the Congress Party and the Bhartiya Janta Party
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the prosecution story as entirely correct and supported by the evidence of PW-2 and two independent witnesses (PWs 3 and 4).
witness_credibility: PW-1 is an injured witness and his presence cannot be disputed. The court found it difficult to believe that PW-1 would have left out the true assailants of his brother. The court also found the presence of PW-2, PW-3, and PW-4 to be credible despite their absence from the FIR.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 24th March 1994; Trial judgment: 23.05.2003; High Court decision: 23.05.2003; Supreme Court decision: 24 February 2011
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: U.R. Lalit, E.M.S. Anam, Fazlin Anam; Counsel for the State: Dinesh Dwivedi, G. Prakash, Beena Prakash, V. Senthil
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Acquittal; High Court: Reversed acquittal of four accused; Supreme Court: Dismissed appeal
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused persons belonged to the Bhartiya Janta Party and that due to political animosity, they formed an unlawful assembly and assaulted PW-1 and his brother with weapons, resulting in the brother's death. The prosecution story was fully supported by the evidence of PW-2 and two independent witnesses (PWs 3 and 4).
defence_argument: The defence argued that the facts of the case did not justify interference by the High Court in an appeal against acquittal. They contended that the Trial Court's findings were not perverse and that the prosecution story was not credible, with doubts about the presence and reliability of the witnesses.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the High Court should not interfere in an appeal against acquittal save in exceptional cases, and that interference is called for only if the findings of the Trial Court are not borne out by the evidence and are perverse.
precedent_relied_upon: Arulvelu and Anr. v. State represented by the Public Prosecutor and Anr. (2009 (10) SCC 206]
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the High Court found the Trial Court's acquittal to be perverse, and the prosecution story was entirely correct and supported by the evidence of the witnesses.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, who were part of an unlawful assembly, assaulted the victim and his brother at a bus stand due to political animosity. The victim sustained grievous injuries and later died in the hospital. The prosecution presented evidence from multiple witnesses, including the victim's brother, who described the incident and the weapons used. The victim's brother was examined by a doctor who found multiple incised wounds on him. The deceased's body was subjected to a post-mortem, which revealed 58 injuries, most of which were incised and cutting wounds. The accused were charged with offenses under Sections 147, 148, 307, 324, and 302 of the IPC. The trial court acquitted all accused, but the High Court reversed the acquittal of four accused, finding the trial court's decision to be perverse. The High Court endorsed the spontaneity of the FIR and found the prosecution's story to be supported by the evidence of multiple witnesses.

title: AK DEVAIAH versus STATE OF KARNATAKA

statutory_provisions: IPC s.304-B, s.498-A; Dowry Prohibition Act s.3, s.4, s.6

physical_harm: The deceased sustained 97% ante-mortem burns and died due to shock as a result of the burns sustained.
number_of_offences: The appellant was charged with offences under Sections 3, 4, and 6 of the Dowry Prohibition Act and Sections 498-A and 304-B of the IPC. The High Court upheld all the charges.
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the evidence of the sister, brother, and sister's husband of the deceased, who consistently deposed about the demand and acceptance of dowry and the deceased being subjected to mental and physical cruelty by the appellant.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses (PWs 1, 2, and 3) as credible, noting their consistent statements about the dowry demand and harassment of the bride, and found their testimony to be reliable in the context of the case.

legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that under Section 304-B of the IPC, a dowry death is presumed to have been caused by the husband or his relatives if the death occurs within seven years of marriage and the deceased was subjected to cruelty or harassment related to dowry demands. title: BADAL MURMU AND ORS. versus STATE OF WEST BENGAL
case_title: Badal Murmu And Ors. v. State of West Bengal
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under section 148 and section 302 r/w section 149
offence_finally_established: culpable homicide not amounting to murder
neutral_facts: The accused and the victim were part of a community where a dispute arose over the theft of a hen by the victim. The accused called the victim to a meeting, where they tied him and his companion to trees and assaulted them with lathis. The victim died as a result of the injuries sustained during the assault. The accused were all present and participated in the beating, but no individual role was ascribed to any of them. The victim's wife and other witnesses observed the incident and provided accounts of the assault. The medical examination indicated that the victim's death was caused by the injuries sustained, but it was not clear which injury was fatal. The accused were armed with lathis and tangies, but the tangies were not used. The prosecution relied on eyewitness accounts and medical evidence to establish the assault and the victim's death.
physical_harm: Deceased was assaulted with lathis leading to his death; fourteen injuries including bruises, abrasions, two rib fractures, and haemotoma under the scalp
number_of_offences: Eleven offences charged; conviction under Section 304 Part II upheld
premeditation_planning: Not found; the court noted that the appellants did not share a common object to murder and did not use sharp weapons
motive: Anger over the theft of a hen and the penalty imposed by the village panchayat
key_evidence_accepted: The evidence of PW-1, PW-3, PW-6 and PW-7 was truthful and was rightly relied upon. They were rustic witnesses and candidly stated all that they had seen. Pertinently, PW-7 did not hesitate to name his brother as one of the assailants. The doctor PW-9 who did the post-mortem stated that the death was caused due to the injuries described by him and that the injuries could be caused by a blunt object like lathi.
witness_credibility: The witnesses were related to the deceased, but the tenor of their evidence was such that it was not possible to say that they have falsely involved the appellants. Their evidence had a ring of truth.

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellants assaulted the deceased with lathis, leading to his death, and that the evidence of the witnesses was truthful and should be relied upon. They claimed that the appellants shared a common object to murder the deceased and that their actions resulted in his death.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, as there was no individual role assigned to any accused, no specific weapon used to cause fatal injuries, and the use of lathis rather than sharp weapons indicated no intent to kill. They also emphasized the socio-economic background of the accused and the trivial nature of the incident.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that if the prosecution cannot establish the common object to murder and the specific role of each accused in causing the fatal injury, then the conviction under Section 302 r/w 149 cannot be sustained. judicial_mitigating_factors: The socio-economic background of the accused, their status as poor tribals, the trivial nature of the incident, and the fact that they had already served 14 years in jail.
other_sentence_order: The sentence already undergone by the accused is directed to be treated as sentence imposed on them under Section 304 Part II of the IPC. The appellants are directed to be released forthwith unless otherwise required in any other case.

title: SHARANJIT KAUR & ANR. versus STATE OF PUNJAB
case_title: SHARANJIT KAUR & ANR. v. STATE OF PUNJAB
trial_court_outcome: Accused denied anticipatory bail
neutral_facts: The accused individuals were alleged to have duped a complainant by taking Rs. 30 lakhs under the pretense of sending his son to America for a permanent job. The complainant paid the amount in several instalments, but the accused failed to fulfill the promise and issued a cheque for Rs. 30 lakhs which was dishonoured due to insufficient funds. The complainant filed a First Information Report (FIR) under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code. The accused challenged the denial of anticipatory bail, arguing that the case should be tried by the Gram Panchayat under the Punjab Panchayati Raj Act.
physical_harm: Not stated
number_of_offences: Number of offences/counts charged: 1; Number of offences finally upheld: 1
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the evidence that the accused duped the complainant of Rs. 30 lakhs and issued a dishonoured cheque, which were serious allegations under Section 420 IPC.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the witnesses by noting that the accused failed to appear before the Gram Panchayat and did not participate in the enquiry proceedings, indicating their non-cooperation.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 03.04.2012; Trial judgment: 23.07.2012; High Court decision: 23.07.2012 and 07.11.2012; Supreme Court decision: July 1, 2013

investigation_status: Investigation conducted by the police authorities; Report under Section 173 Cr.P.C. filed; Case transferred to Gram Panchayat or other subordinate court by the Magistrate

prosecution_argument: The respondent-State argued that in view of serious allegations against the appellants who cheated the complainant's son and committed fraud by taking his money, the prosecuting authority is entitled to proceed under the provisions of the IPC, and that the police have the authority to investigate the offence and submit a report to the Magistrate.

sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the investigation is to be conducted by the police authorities only and the offence of Section 420 IPC where the allegations are of a serious nature and the appellants duped the complainant of Rs. 30 lakhs should be tried by the regular criminal court only and not by the Gram Panchayat.

The accused challenged the denial of anticipatory bail, arguing that the case should be tried by the Gram Panchayat under the Punjab Panchayati Raj Act. The victim's brother, PW-4, provided testimony that was later found to be false, as the accused had brought the victim to the hospital.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 10,000/- and rigorous imprisonment for one year in default; rigorous imprisonment for two years and fine of Rs. 2,000/- and rigorous imprisonment for six months in default

number_of_offences: Four accused charged; four accused finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the dying declaration made by the deceased to the magistrate, noting that the doctor's certification of her fitness to make the statement was crucial and that the magistrate's testimony was not to be discarded without proper context.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the witnesses, particularly PW-4, as being influenced by the accused, and noted that his testimony was false due to the records from PGIMS, Rohtak.
trial_duration: The trial court acquitted the accused, the High Court convicted them, and the Supreme Court upheld the conviction.

legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a dying declaration recorded in the presence of a medical officer and with proper certification of the deceased's fitness is admissible and cannot be discarded merely due to the extent of injuries, unless there is clear evidence of the deceased's incapacity.

title: ACHHAR SINGH versus STATE OF HIMACHAL PRADESH

title: DAUVARAM NIRMALKAR versus STATE OF CHHATTISGARH
case_title: Dauvaram Nirmalkar v. State of Chhattisgarh
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.304 Part I; Exception 1 to s.300
confession: Confession admitted to identify the accused as the maker of the report and to admit facts discovered in consequence of such information
aggravating_circumstances: Alcohol addiction of the deceased, constant torment and abuse, final provocative act
mitigating_circumstances: Loss of self-control due to grave and sudden provocation, no premeditation

neutral_facts: The accused, who was the brother of the deceased, was involved in a violent incident where the deceased suffered fatal injuries. The deceased had a history of alcohol addiction and had previously tormented, abused, and threatened the accused. On the night of the incident, the deceased consumed alcohol and told the accused to leave the house, warning that he would kill him if he did not. The accused, who had attempted suicide by holding live electrical wires, lost self-control due to the sudden and grave provocation from the deceased. The accused inflicted fatal injuries on the deceased using a pick-axe. The accused's actions were deemed to be a result of temporary loss of self-control rather than premeditation. 1,000, or simple imprisonment for six months if the fine was not paid.

motive: Deceased's habitual abuse and threats towards the appellant
key_evidence_accepted: The fact that the appellant and the deceased were together the night when the deceased suffered the fatal injuries is established and proven. The chain of facts and circumstances established beyond doubt bars that the appellant and no other person was the perpetrator who had inflicted the injuries on his brother.
witness_credibility: The public witnesses, though declared hostile, have more or less in unison deposed that the appellant and the deceased used to stay in separate rooms at the same house. Their testimonies are important as they were present in the house at the time of the incident.

investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant caused the death of his brother due to grave and sudden provocation, and that the deceased had a history of abusing and threatening the appellant. The deceased had consumed alcohol and told the appellant to leave the house, otherwise he would kill him, leading to a sudden loss of self-control by the appellant.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the appellant's actions were a result of grave and sudden provocation, and that the deceased's abusive behavior over time led to a loss of self-control. The appellant had tried to commit suicide by holding live electrical wires, indicating a temporary loss of self-control rather than premeditation.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle of Exception 1 to Section 300 of the IPC, which recognizes that culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, deprived of the power of self-control by grave and sudden provocation, causes the death of the person who gave the provocation or another person by mistake or accident.
precedent_relied_upon: K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra [1962] 1 Suppl. SCR 567; Budhi Singh v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2012) 13 SCC 663 : [2012] 11 SCR 848; Aghnoo Nagesia v. State of Bihar [1966] 1 SCR 134

judicial_mitigating_factors: The court considered the appellant's prior incarceration for over 10 years and the fact that the act was a result of grave and sudden provocation, leading to a temporary loss of self-control.

neutral_facts_raw: The accused, who was the brother of the deceased, was involved in a violent incident where the deceased suffered fatal injuries. The accused, who had attempted suicide by holding live electrical wires, lost self-control due to the sudden and grave provocation from the deceased. The accused inflicted fatal injuries on the deceased using a pick-axe. The accused's actions were deemed to be a result of temporary loss of self-control rather than premeditation. The accused was initially convicted under s.302 IPC for murder, but the conviction was converted to s.304 Part I IPC under Exception 1 to s.300 IPC due to the provocation and loss of self-control. The accused was sentenced to imprisonment for 10 years, a fine of Rs. 1,000, or simple imprisonment for six months if the fine was not paid.

aggravating_circumstances: Motive established, use of vehicle, dismemberment of body, conspiracy

The witnesses PW-3, 4, and 5, who were relatives of the deceased, witnessed the incident and described the overt acts of the accused, particularly A-1, A-2, and A-7. The delay in lodging the FIR was explained by the fact that the deceased was taken to the hospital, and the lack of a dying declaration was justified as the deceased remained unconscious until death.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution's case should be disbelieved because the witnesses PW-3, 4, and 5 were relatives of the deceased, the delay in lodging the FIR was unexplained, no dying declaration was recorded, and the injuries sustained by some accused were not properly explained by the prosecution.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the mere relationship of witnesses to the deceased does not invalidate their testimony, and that the prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, especially when the witnesses are credible and their testimonies are corroborated by other evidence.
precedent_relied_upon: Abdul Rashid Abdul Rahiman Patel and Ors. v. State of Maharashtra (2007) 9 SCC 1

title: RAM SINGH versus THE STATE OF U.P.
case_title: Ram Singh v. The State of U.P.
aggravating_circumstances: Non-recovery of weapon, non-examination of ballistic expert
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.301/302 and s.307 IPC
neutral_facts: The prosecution alleged that the accused, Ram Singh, and another accused, Lala Ram, were involved in a fatal shooting incident. The victim, Dulli, was sitting on a cot in the courtyard of the accused's house. PW-1, the son of the deceased, and his brother Desh Raj were also present. According to the prosecution, Lala Ram instigated Ram Singh to fire at PW-1, but the bullet struck Dulli, causing her death. The police recovered some cartridges and pellets from the scene and the victim's body, but the weapon used was not recovered. The prosecution relied on eyewitness accounts and medical evidence, but there were inconsistencies in the testimonies of the witnesses.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment / Rigorous imprisonment for five years
physical_harm: Gunshot injury resulting in death
number_of_offences: Two offences/counts charged; both upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the prosecution failed to recover the weapon of crime, obtain a ballistic opinion, and examine a ballistic expert, which significantly weakened the prosecution's case.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses' evidence as suffering from serious lacunae and could not be said to be credible.
trial_duration: Trial judgment: 05.02.2018; High Court decision: 05.02.2018; Supreme Court decision: 21 February 2024
legal_representation: Pradeep Kumar Mathur, Chiranjeev Johri, Chandra Nand Jha, M.K. Tiwari, Sitesh Kumar, Arvind Kumar, Advs. for the Appellant; Rana Mukherjee, Sr. Adv., Samarth Mohanty, Ankit Goel, Advs. for the Respondent
investigation_status: Charge sheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Non-recovery of the weapon of crime, non-examination of ballistic expert, non-obtaining of ballistic opinion
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction and sentence imposed; High Court: Conviction and sentence confirmed; Supreme Court: Conviction and sentence set aside
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant Ram Singh was responsible for the death of the deceased, Dulli, by firing a shot from a country made pistol at her. They relied on the testimony of PW-1, the son of the deceased, and other witnesses, including the police investigation and post-mortem report. The prosecution claimed that the evidence, including the eyewitness accounts, was sufficient to prove the appellant's guilt beyond all reasonable doubt.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution's case was flawed due to glaring inconsistencies in the eyewitness accounts, the non-recovery of the weapon of crime, and the failure to obtain a ballistic report or examine a ballistic expert. They contended that the evidence was not credible and that the trial court and High Court erred in convicting the appellant while acquitting the co-accused Lala Ram on the same set of evidence.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that non-recovery of the weapon of crime and non-examination of a ballistic expert do not automatically invalidate the prosecution's case, but if the evidence suffers from glaring inconsistencies and material witnesses are not examined, the omission may be fatal to the prosecution's case. The court also emphasized the principle of parity, stating that similar evidence against two accused cannot result in one being convicted and the other acquitted.
precedent_relied_upon: Javed Shaukat Ali Qureshi Vs. State of Gujarat, [2023] 12 SCR 220 : (2023) 9 SCC 164; Munna Lal Vs. sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the prosecution failed to prove the appellant's guilt beyond all reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court found the evidence to be inconsistent and not credible, and the non-recovery of the weapon, non-examination of the ballistic expert, and failure to examine material witnesses rendered the prosecution's case insufficient to justify conviction.
neutral_facts_raw: The prosecution alleged that the accused, Ram Singh, and another accused, Lala Ram, were involved in a fatal shooting incident. The victim, Dulli, was sitting on a cot in the courtyard of the accused's house. PW-1, the son of the deceased, and his brother Desh Raj were also present. According to the prosecution, Lala Ram instigated Ram Singh to fire at PW-1, but the bullet struck Dulli, causing her death. The police recovered some cartridges and pellets from the scene and the victim's body, but the weapon used was not recovered. The prosecution relied on eyewitness accounts and medical evidence, but there were inconsistencies in the testimonies of the witnesses. The trial court acquitted Lala Ram, while convicting Ram Singh. The High Court upheld the conviction, but the Supreme Court found the evidence insufficient and overturned the conviction.

title: KIRITI PAL versus STATE OF WEST BENGAL
case_title: KIRITI PAL V. STATE OF WEST BENGAL
aggravating_circumstances: Proximity of time between deceased's last seen alive and death, failure to explain separation, threatening conduct, recovery of weapon at instance of accused
trial_court_outcome: Convicted and sentenced to death
high_court_outcome: Upheld conviction under s.302, modified death sentence to life imprisonment
neutral_facts: The accused, a man who had developed intimacy with the deceased woman, was last seen with her on the day she died. The deceased was found dead the following day in a remote location. The accused failed to explain how they parted ways, and his subsequent conduct included threatening others. A weapon was recovered at his instance, and there was no evidence to establish the involvement of the other accused in the crime. The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence, including the time gap between the deceased's last seen alive and her death, the absence of a satisfactory explanation for her death, and the accused's behavior after the incident.

The subsequent conduct of A-1 threatening A-4 and PW-7 was also a relevant circumstance. The recovery of the crime weapon at the instance of A-1 was yet another incriminating circumstance in the chain which led to the conclusion pointing to the guilt of A-1.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, particularly PWs 6, 7, and 10, whose evidence established that the victim-deceased was last seen alive in the company of A-1 on the fateful evening. legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that in cases of circumstantial evidence, the circumstances must be fully established beyond any reasonable doubt, form a complete chain pointing to the guilt of the accused, and be consistent with the hypothesis of guilt. title: PARUBAI versus THE STATE OF MAHARASHTRA
case_title: Parubai v. The State of Maharashtra
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 and s.436
neutral_facts: The accused, Parubai, was living in a house with her husband, Gulab, and his first wife, Mandabai, along with their children. On the night of August 2/3, 2006, a fire broke out in the house, engulfing it in flames. Parubai exited the house unscathed, while Mandabai and her daughter, Nikita, were burned and later died from their injuries. Their son, Akash, died in the fire. The father-in-law of Parubai, Gajanan, reported the incident and implicated Parubai. The prosecution argued that Parubai had a motive due to her second marriage and the arrangement for maintenance in favor of Mandabai.

title: MUNNAWAR AND ORS. versus STATE OF U.P. ETC.
case_title: Munnawar and Ors. v. State of U.P. Etc.
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted of Section 302, convicted under Section 307
neutral_facts: The accused fired a shot at the victim during an incident that occurred while the victim and his brother were on their way to a court hearing. The victim was seriously injured and taken to a hospital, where he was examined by a doctor. A dying declaration was recorded by an executive magistrate, which detailed the identity of the assailants, the weapon used, and the site of the injury. The victim succumbed to his injuries after five days, with the cause of death attributed to septicemia resulting from the gunshot wound. The prosecution relied on the testimony of the victim's brother and other witnesses, as well as the dying declaration and medical evidence.
offence_severity: Minimum 10 years, Maximum Life Imprisonment or Death
physical_harm: Death of victim due to septicemia caused by gunshot injuries
number_of_offences: Three counts charged, two upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The dying declaration recorded by the Executive Magistrate gave full details as to the identity of the assailants, the weapons used, the site of the injury and the fact that he was brought to the hospital by a neighbour and his elder brother who were accompanying him at the time of incident. The doctor who was looking after the deceased when the dying declaration was recorded gave a certificate that he was fully conscious and lucid at the time of its recording.
witness_credibility: The promptness in recording of FIR would belie the doubt as to the presence of eyewitness-informant at the place of incident. The presence of the two eye witnesses is accepted as they were accompanying the deceased to court and the promptness of the FIR reflects their presence.
trial_duration: The incident took place on 20th May 2000. The FIR was lodged on 20th May 2000 at 12 noon. The trial court judgment was on 8th August 2007. The High Court decision was on 8th August 2007. The Supreme Court judgment was on 5th May 2010.
legal_representation: Sushil Kumar, Manoj Prasad, Aditya Kumar for the Appellants. T.N. Singh, Rajiv Dubey, Kamlendra Mishra for the Respondent.
investigation_status: FIR lodged on 20th May 2000 at 12 noon. Charge-sheet filed. Trial completed.
appeal_history: Trial court acquitted the appellants of offence under Section 302 IPC but convicted them under Section 307 IPC. High Court convicted appellants for offence under Section 302/149 IPC. Supreme Court dismissed the appeals.
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the deceased, along with PW-1 and PW-2, was on the way to court to attend a case. The appellants armed with a pistol fired a shot at the deceased and then ran away. The deceased was seriously injured and taken to the hospital. The FIR was lodged promptly, and the presence of eyewitnesses was confirmed. The injuries were grievous and sufficient to cause death, and the dying declaration was reliable.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the first dying declaration recorded by the police officer did not have the endorsement of a doctor and was therefore unreliable. They also claimed that the second dying declaration was not properly endorsed and that the medical evidence showed the death was due to septicemia caused by the injuries, not the initial gunshot wound. They further argued that the eye witnesses were not present at the scene and that the case should be under Section 307 IPC.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a dying declaration recorded by a Magistrate duly endorsed by a Doctor should not be discarded unless there are suspicious circumstances. The Court emphasized that the reliability of the dying declaration depends on the facts of the case and the evidence produced.
precedent_relied_upon: Balak Ram v. State of U.P. 1975(3) SCC 219; K. Ramachandra Reddy & Anr. v. The Public Prosecutor 1976(3) SCC 618
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the injuries were grievous and sufficient to cause death, and the dying declaration was reliable. The Court found that the trial court had erred in concluding that the doctor's negligence caused the death, and the High Court's conviction under Section 302/149 IPC was upheld.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused fired a shot at the victim during an incident that occurred while the victim and his brother were on their way to a court hearing. The victim was seriously injured and taken to a hospital, where he was examined by a doctor. A dying declaration was recorded by an executive magistrate, which detailed the identity of the assailants, the weapon used, and the site of the injury. The victim succumbed to his injuries after five days, with the cause of death attributed to septicemia resulting from the gunshot wound. The prosecution relied on the testimony of the victim's brother and other witnesses, as well as the dying declaration and medical evidence. The trial court acquitted the accused of murder but convicted them under Section 307 for causing grievous harm. The High Court overturned this decision and convicted the accused under Section 302/149 for murder.

witness_credibility: PW-13, the beat constable, was on duty and his presence at the incident location was natural. His statement that he was assigned to duty at the place of the incident was not cast in doubt. The mere fact that panch witnesses turned hostile is no reason to discredit the prosecution's case.

legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that an appellate court is justified in reversing an order of acquittal if it suffers from perversity and results in a miscarriage of justice, as established in K Gopal Reddy v. premeditation_planning: Court found premeditated intention as the accused were armed and present at the scene with a clear plan
motive: Evil eye kept on the wife of one of the accused by the deceased

investigation_status: FIR registered (No.79/2015 dated 03.11.2015), charge sheet filed, trial completed

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that there was a common intention among all the accused to cause the death of the victim, supported by the presence of all four accused at the scene with weapons and the testimony of the wife of the deceased.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the appellants only held the deceased without participating in the actual assault or using a weapon, and thus should not be held liable for the murder.

neutral_facts_raw: The accused and the victim were relatives with a prior incident between them. On the night of the incident, the victim and his wife woke up, and while the wife prepared for cooking, the victim went to attend to nature's call. The wife heard the victim shouting and ran to the scene, where she saw two of the accused assaulting the victim with an axe while the other two held him. The victim was taken to the hospital and declared dead. The accused were charged with murder under Section 302 of the IPC read with Section 34. title: STATE THROUGH THE INSPECTOR OF POLICE versus LALY @ MANIKANDAN & ANOTHER ETC
petitioner: STATE THROUGH THE INSPECTOR OF POLICE
case_title: State through the Inspector of Police v. Laly @ Manikandan & Another Etc.
trial_court_outcome: Convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 1,000/- each
offence_finally_established: Murder under Section 302 IPC and Section 302 r/w 34 IPC
neutral_facts: The accused were tried for the murder of the deceased. The prosecution case was that the deceased, along with PW1 and another person, were traveling in a car when the accused attacked them, causing injury to the deceased on the right shoulder. The deceased then tried to run away and reached a shed, where the accused chased him, entered the shed, and caused further injuries leading to the deceased's death. PW1, an eyewitness, was present in the car during the initial attack and later saw the accused enter the shed and cause injuries to the deceased. PW1's testimony was fully supported and cross-examined, and the court found no reason to disbelieve his account. The prosecution also presented medical evidence and statements from witnesses, though some witnesses contradicted the prosecution's timeline and details.
offence_severity: Death (Section 302) with life imprisonment and fine
physical_harm: Injuries caused to the deceased resulting in death
number_of_offences: Three counts charged, three upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the deposition of PW1 as the key evidence, recognizing him as the sole eye witness to the occurrence at both places and finding no reason to disbelieve or doubt his credibility.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses, finding that PW1's testimony was fully supported and credible despite thorough cross-examination, while other witnesses either contradicted the prosecution's case or were not examined.
trial_duration: The trial judgment was passed on 12.06.2018 by the High Court of Madras, and the Supreme Court decision was on 14.10.2022.
legal_representation: Dr. Joseph Aristotle S., Ms. Nupur Sharma, Shobhit Dwivedi, Sanjeev Kumar Mahara, Advs. for the Appellant; Rao Ranjit, Adv. for the Respondents
investigation_status: FIR registered on 31.07.2013, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court convicted the accused; High Court acquitted the accused; Supreme Court set aside the High Court's acquittal and restored the trial court's conviction.
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that PW1, the sole eye witness, provided reliable testimony and fully supported the case. The incident occurred in two parts, with PW1 present at both locations and witnessing the accused causing injuries to the deceased. The prosecution emphasized that the recovery of the weapon is not a sine qua non for conviction and that contradictions in the FIR/complaint timing do not justify acquittal.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the original complainant, Mahendran, was not examined, and other independent witnesses were not examined. They also claimed that the recovery of the weapon was not proved and that there were contradictions in the deposition of PW1 regarding the injuries caused. These factors, they argued, undermined the reliability of PW1 and justified acquittal.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a conviction can be based on the deposition of a sole eye witness if the witness is found trustworthy and reliable. It also emphasized that the recovery of the weapon is not a sine qua non for conviction and that contradictions in FIR/complaint timing do not justify acquittal.
precedent_relied_upon: Krishna Mochi v. State of Bihar (2002) 6 SCC 81; Kunju Muhammed v. State of Kerala, (2004) 9 SCC 193
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the High Court's acquittal was deemed unsustainable. The Supreme Court restored the trial court's conviction and sentence, finding the prosecution's case based on PW1's reliable testimony sufficient for conviction.
other_sentence_order: The accused were directed to surrender to the concerned Jail authorities/Court to undergo the sentence imposed by the trial court within six weeks. If they failed to do so, the concerned Superintendent of Police/Court was directed to take them into custody.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused were tried for the murder of the deceased. The prosecution case was that the deceased, along with PW1 and another person, were traveling in a car when the accused attacked them, causing injury to the deceased on the right shoulder. The deceased then tried to run away and reached a shed, where the accused chased him, entered the shed, and caused further injuries leading to the deceased's death. PW1, an eyewitness, was present in the car during the initial attack and later saw the accused enter the shed and cause injuries to the deceased. PW1's testimony was fully supported and cross-examined, and the court found no reason to disbelieve his account. The prosecution also presented medical evidence and statements from witnesses, though some witnesses contradicted the prosecution's timeline and details. The trial court convicted the accused based on PW1's testimony and the evidence, but the High Court acquitted them, citing inconsistencies in the FIR registration, lack of examination of the original complainant, and contradictions in witness statements. The Supreme Court overturned the High Court's acquittal, finding PW1's testimony reliable and sufficient for conviction despite the absence of weapon recovery and some contradictions in the FIR timing.

title: KATTUKULANGARA MADHAVAN (DEAD) THR. LRS. versus MAJEED & ORS.
case_title: KATTUKULANGARA MADHAVAN (DEAD) THR. LRS. v. MAJEED & ORS.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 rlw s.149; IPC s.326 rlw s.149
aggravating_circumstances: Political rivalry, unlawful assembly, multiple injuries, presence in unlawful assembly
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302/149 IPC, sentenced to life imprisonment; some acquitted
high_court_outcome: Set aside conviction of some accused, acquitted others
neutral_facts: The deceased was part of a bus traveling through a junction where an unlawful assembly of individuals from opposing political parties had gathered. The assembly's common object was to attack any rival party supporter. The deceased was attacked and killed during this incident. The accused were part of the assembly and were involved in the attack, with some individuals using sticks and a knife to inflict injuries. The prosecution relied on eyewitness accounts and medical evidence to establish the incident and the involvement of the accused in the unlawful assembly.
offence_severity: Minimum 6 years to maximum life imprisonment
physical_harm: Death caused by stabbing and beating with sticks causing simple injuries on non-vital parts
number_of_offences: 21 accused charged; 16 convictions upheld, 5 acquitted
key_evidence_accepted: PW3 who was an independent witness and was believed by both the lower courts had given a vivid description of incident - PW4 was an eye witness and was believed by trial court - The evidence on record showed that the deceased and accused belong to two political parties opposed to each other - There were three other incidents of clashes between the rival groups - The accused along with others assembled and were searching for rival party workers travelling in the buses that were passing through the junction - The common object of the members of the unlawful assembly was to attack any rival party supporter who was passing through the junction - The deceased was in the bus and he was killed in the attack
witness_credibility: PW3 was an independent witness and was believed by both the lower courts. PW4 was an eye witness and was believed by the trial court. The High Court disbelieved PW6 and the evidence of PW5. The Trial Court held that PW4 was also a credible witness and there was no material contradiction brought out in the evidence of PW5.
trial_duration: The trial judgment was dated 05.09.2005, and the Supreme Court decision was on 30 March 2017.
legal_representation: Basant R., Sr. Adv., Raghenth Basant, Kartik Ashok, James Joseph, Misha! Johari, Senthil Jagadeesan, Ms. Bina Madhavan, Advs. for the Appellants. Siddharth Luthra, Sr. Adv., Deepak Prakash, Anoopam N. Prasad, Ali Chaudhury, Swati Ghildiyal, Kuna! Singh, Subhash Chandran, Ms. Usha Nandini, G. Prakash, Jishnu M. L., Mrs. Priyanka Prakash, Mrs. Beenu Prakash, Manu Srinath, Ms. Bina Madhavan, Ms. Usha Nandini V, Advs. for the Respondents.
investigation_status: FIR registered on 10.03.1993 under Sections 143, 147, 148, 341, 324, 302/149 IPC. Private complaint filed on 01.04.1994. Charge sheet filed after investigation.
appeal_history: Trial court acquitted some accused. High Court overturned some acquittals and convictions. Supreme Court allowed appeals against acquittals and upheld convictions.
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused were part of an unlawful assembly with a common object to attack any rival party supporter, and that the deceased was killed in the attack. defence_argument: The defence argued that the High Court erred in not considering the evidence of PW4, which could be used for corroboration. They also claimed that the accused did not have a common object to commit murder and that the prosecution failed to prove the common object of the unlawful assembly.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the mere presence in an unlawful assembly may vicariously fasten criminal liability under Section 149 IPC, and that the conduct of the accused determines whether they shared the common object of the assembly.
precedent_relied_upon: Lalji v. State of U.P. (1989) 1 SCC 437; State of UP v. Dan Singh (1997) 3 SCC 747; Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade v. State of Maharashtra (1973) 2 SCC 793
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed considering that the incident occurred in 1993, the accused attacked the deceased with sticks causing simple injuries on non-vital parts, and their conviction under Section 326/149 IPC met the ends of justice.
other_sentence_order: A3, A4, A14, A15 and A18 were sentenced to 7 years imprisonment under Section 326/149 IPC. The acquittal of A5 to A13, A16 and A17 was upheld. Criminal Appeal No. 661 of 2006 and 400 of 2006 were dismissed.

The accused were part of the assembly and were involved in the attack, with some individuals using sticks and a knife to inflict injuries. The prosecution relied on eyewitness accounts and medical evidence to establish the incident and the involvement of the accused in the unlawful assembly.

title: GOVINDARAJU@ GOVINDA versus STATE BY SRIRAMAPURAM P.S. & ANR.
case_title: GOVINDARAJU@ GOVINDA v. STATE BY SRIRAMAPURAM P.S.
trial_court_outcome: Acquittal
high_court_outcome: Convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment and fine of Rs.10,000/-
neutral_facts: The prosecution alleged that on the fateful day, a police officer witnessed three individuals chasing another person. The chased individual fell on the road and was stabbed by the three individuals. The police officer, who was on a motorcycle, could not stop the assailants and they fled. The police officer then took the victim to the hospital where he was declared dead. The police officer checked the victim's pockets and found an identity card, which led to the victim's identification. The police officer then lodged a complaint, and an FIR was filed. The investigating officer examined witnesses and recovered weapons, which were sent for forensic analysis.
physical_harm: Injuries caused resulting in death
number_of_offences: Number of offences/counts charged: 1; Number finally upheld: 1
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the prosecution's case suffered from proven improbabilities, infirmities, contradictions, and the statement of the sole witness, the Police Officer, PW1, is not reliable and worthy of credence.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as unreliable and not credible, particularly the sole eye-witness, the police officer, whose testimony lacked corroboration and was found to be not trustworthy.
trial_duration: The trial court acquitted both the appellant-'GV' and 'GR' for an offence under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC. The State preferred a leave to appeal before the High Court. The High Court declined the leave to appeal against the judgment of acquittal in favour of 'GV' and granted the leave to appeal against 'GR'. 'GR' was convicted under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to imprisonment for life and fine of Rs.10,000/-
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused and the State in the Supreme Court: Not stated
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Non-examination of material witnesses as also persons from the forensic laboratory - Medical Evidence also not supporting the prosecution case - Defect in the recovery - Recovery witnesses turned hostile
appeal_history: Trial court: Acquittal; High Court: Granted leave to appeal against 'GR' and convicted 'GR'; Supreme Court: Allowed the appeal, acquitted the appellant
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the sole eye-witness, a police officer, saw three accused chasing and then inflicting injuries upon the deceased, and that the recovery of weapons and medical evidence supported their case. They also claimed that the absence of independent witnesses and the non-examination of material witnesses created reasonable doubt.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution's case suffered from proven improbabilities, infirmities, and contradictions. The testimony of the sole eye-witness, the police officer, was not reliable and lacked corroboration. The recovery of weapons was defective, and the non-examination of material witnesses created reasonable doubt.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that an appellate court has the power to re-appreciate and reweigh evidence, but interference is justifiable only when the trial court's judgment was perverse in law or appreciation of evidence. The court also emphasized the presumption of innocence and the need for the prosecution to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
precedent_relied_upon: Girja Prasad (Dead) By LRs. v. State of MP. (2007) 7 SCC 625: 2007 (9) SCR 483; State of Rajasthan v. Shera Ram alias Vishnu Dutta (2012) 1 SCC 602; Takhaji Hiraji v. Thakore Kubersing Chamansing and Ors. [(2001) 6 SCC 145]; Yakub lsmailbhai Patel v. State of Gujarat [(2,004) 12 SCC 229]
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the High Court found the trial court's judgment to be perverse in law or appreciation of evidence, and the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
other_sentence_order: The appellant was acquitted and set at liberty, with his bail and surety bonds discharged.
neutral_facts_raw: The prosecution alleged that on the fateful day, a police officer witnessed three individuals chasing another person. The chased individual fell on the road and was stabbed by the three individuals. The police officer, who was on a motorcycle, could not stop the assailants and they fled. The police officer then took the victim to the hospital where he was declared dead. The police officer checked the victim's pockets and found an identity card, which led to the victim's identification. The police officer then lodged a complaint, and an FIR was filed. The investigating officer examined witnesses and recovered weapons, which were sent for forensic analysis. The trial court acquitted the accused, and the High Court initially convicted one of the accused. The Supreme Court reviewed the case, noting the lack of reliable evidence, the absence of corroborating witnesses, and the unreliability of the sole eyewitness, the police officer. The Supreme Court ultimately acquitted the accused, finding the prosecution's case to be improbable and lacking in credibility.

title: PHULEL SINGH versus STATE OF HARAYANA
case_title: Phulel Singh v. State of Haryana
trial_court_outcome: Convicted of dowry death
high_court_outcome: Partly allowed appeal, acquitted accused no.1
neutral_facts: The accused, who was the husband of the deceased, was alleged to have harassed the deceased due to insufficient dowry. The deceased was admitted to a hospital with severe burns, and a dying declaration was recorded by an Executive Magistrate. The declaration stated that the accused had poured kerosene on her and set her on fire. The deceased's relatives applied for the recording of the statement, and the magistrate recorded it after examining the deceased's fitness. The prosecution relied on the dying declaration and the testimony of the deceased's relatives and a village Sarpanch to establish harassment due to dowry demands. However, the evidence was questioned for its reliability and voluntariness, and the deceased's short temper and the absence of the accused on the day of the incident were noted.
physical_harm: Burn injuries with 91% burns on body
number_of_offences: Charges under Sections 302 and 304-B of IPC; conviction under Section 304-B upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the dying declaration (Ex. P.L.) is not free from doubt and questioned its reliability due to potential tutoring and lack of voluntariness.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses, including the relatives of the deceased and the Sarpanch, with skepticism, noting that their evidence lacked concrete support for the prosecution's case regarding dowry harassment.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 5th November 1991; Trial judgment: 14th September 1999; High Court decision: 24th July 2009; Supreme Court decision: 27th September 2023
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Rajul Bhargav, Sr. Adv., Rajiv K. Garg, Ashish Garg, Lalit Nagar, T. L. Garg, Advs.; Counsel for the State: Samar Vijay Singh, Raj Singh Rana, Keshav Mittal, Ms. Sabarni Som, Aman Dev Sharma, Pankaj Kumar Singh, Advs.
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction and sentence upheld; High Court: Partly allowed the appeal, acquitted accused no.1, upheld conviction of appellant; Supreme Court: Appeal allowed, conviction quashed, appellant acquitted
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant harassed the deceased on account of insufficiency of dowry, leading to her death by burning. defence_argument: The defence argued that the dying declaration was not reliable and was tutored by the deceased's relatives. They also contended that there was no evidence to prove harassment on account of non-fulfillment of dowry, and the case under Section 304-B of the IPC was not made out.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a conviction based on a dying declaration must be supported by evidence that the declaration is trustworthy, reliable, and free from doubt.
precedent_relied_upon: Makhan Singh v. State of Haryana 2022 SCC OnLine SC 1019
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, who was the husband of the deceased, was alleged to have harassed the deceased due to insufficient dowry. The deceased was admitted to a hospital with severe burns, and a dying declaration was recorded by an Executive Magistrate. The declaration stated that the accused had poured kerosene on her and set her on fire. The deceased's relatives applied for the recording of the statement, and the magistrate recorded it after examining the deceased's fitness. The prosecution relied on the dying declaration and the testimony of the deceased's relatives and a village Sarpanch to establish harassment due to dowry demands. title: RAM PAL @ BUNDA versus STATE OF HARYANA
case_title: RAM PAL @ BUNDA v. STATE OF HARYANA
aggravating_circumstances: Inimical relationship with the family of the victim, absence from the village for two days, running away from the scene of crime
trial_court_outcome: Convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment and 10 years rigorous imprisonment
neutral_facts: The prosecution presented circumstantial evidence, including the presence of the accused at the scene of the crime immediately after the incident, his absence from the village for two days, and medical evidence indicating that the victim was subjected to sexual intercourse before her death. offence_severity: Death (Section 302) - Minimum 10 years, Maximum Life Imprisonment; Rape (Section 376) - Minimum 10 years, Maximum Life Imprisonment

number_of_offences: Two offences (Sections 302 and 376) were charged and both were upheld.
premeditation_planning: The court found premeditation/planning based on the accused's past grievances and his expressed intent to take revenge.
motive: The motive was the accused's past misbehavior and grudge against the family of the victim, particularly due to an incident in a Panchayat where he was reprimanded and forced to apologize.
key_evidence_accepted: Medical evidence revealed that the victim was subjected to sexual intercourse before her death, and PW-10, the mother of the victim, found the accused present at the scene of crime immediately after the occurrence.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the witnesses, including PW-10 and PW-11, as their statements were corroborated and supported the prosecution version.
post_offence_conduct: The accused ran away from the scene of occurrence without responding to the queries of PW-10 and remained absconding for two days.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 18.2.2005; Trial judgment: 07.09.2011; High Court decision: Not stated; Supreme Court decision: April 11, 2013
legal_representation: R.K. Talwar, David Rao, K. Kaushik, Chander Shekhar Ashri for the Appellant; A Kamal Mohan Gupta for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction and sentence confirmed; High Court: Conviction and sentence confirmed; Supreme Court: Appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused was present at the scene of the crime immediately after the occurrence, ran away without responding to the queries of the victim's mother, remained absconding for two days, and had an inimical relationship with the victim's family, which supported the prosecution's version of the case.
defence_argument: The accused claimed he was falsely implicated due to inimical relations with the family of the victim, but did not present any evidence to support his defense.
legal_principle_applied: The court applied the principle that circumstantial evidence can be sufficient to convict if it forms a complete chain of circumstances that support the prosecution's case and there are no missing links.
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
sentencing_rationale: The sentence was imposed because the prosecution's version was fully supported by the evidence, the accused did not present any defense, and the motive was justified based on the inimical relationship with the victim's family.

The accused did not provide any evidence in his defense. The trial court found that the accused had a motive due to his past misbehavior towards the victim's family, which led to a grudge and a desire for revenge. The medical evidence showed that the victim died from asphyxia due to strangulation, with signs of sexual intercourse prior to her death. The accused was not present during the investigation and was arrested two days after the incident.

title: KARTHI @ KARTHICK versus STATE REP. BY INSPECTOR OF POLICE, TAMIL NADU
respondent: STATE REP. BY INSPECTOR OF POLICE, TAMIL NADU
case_title: Karthi @ Karthick v. State Rep. by Inspector of Police, Tamil Nadu
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under Sections 376 and 417 IPC
neutral_facts: The accused, a male, had an unwilling sexual relationship with the victim, a female, who was alone in her house.
